title: Edmund and the Postcards
premise: When a demolition notice arrives for the fading Hotel Miramar, former restaurant critic Ines Almeida — who lost her sense of taste after her sister's unexplained death — is hired to write the building's obituary. Behind her childhood wardrobe she finds a box of forty years of undelivered letters, including ones her sister wrote to her, never sent, revealing that the sister's death was covered up by the hotel's beloved owner to protect a kitchen boy who is now the city's most powerful restaurateur. Ines must choose between exposing the truth and preserving the loyalty of everyone who sheltered her; in the end, she reads the letters aloud in the empty dining room the night before demolition, tells the truth in her final review, and finally tastes a spoonful of soup — grief, at last, with flavor.
about_author: Edmund Pemberton is the pen name of a former line cook turned archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the ephemera of condemned buildings. He writes about the objects people leave behind when they cannot say what they mean.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A scathing, hollow review; her editor notes she hasn't described a taste in three years. She accepts the Hotel Miramar obituary commission to avoid a prestigious tasting menu. Emotional beat: numbness disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Forty Years, Undelivered
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Packing her childhood room in the hotel, she finds the box behind the wardrobe: letters addressed to staff, guests, and her family, all stamped, none sent. The handwriting on the oldest one is her sister Lucia's. Beat: the past physically intrudes.

chapters.title: The Kitchen Boy
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She tracks the letters' author to Aurelio Sanches, once a kitchen boy, now owner of the city's grandest restaurant. He receives her coldly, recognizing the box on sight. Beat: fear beneath charm — the first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: What Lucia Wrote
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, interleaved with Lucia's letters from 1979. Lucia describes a night in the hotel kitchen: a fire, a locked service door, a boy who survived because Lucia let him out first. Beat: Ines realizes her sister's death was not an accident but a choice — and a cover-up.

chapters.title: The Owner's Version
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Ines interviews the aging hotel owner, Dona Beatriz, who tells a noble version — the fire, the sacrifice, the silence that protected a refugee boy with no papers. Beat: loyalty and truth begin to pull in opposite directions.

chapters.title: A Table for Two
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Aurelio invites her to dine, hoping to buy her silence with nostalgia and flattery. She tastes nothing; he confesses he has cooked for her memory for forty years. Beat: guilt and tenderness entangle; the enemy becomes human.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Dona Beatriz's POV. The wrecking crew arrives early; the letters' existence leaks to a hungry young journalist. Beatriz burns nothing and confesses nothing, but begins writing her own unsent letter. Beat: the machinery of erasure accelerates.

chapters.title: The Last Review
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The journalist offers her the exposé; Aurelio begs her to let the dead stay buried; Beatriz asks only for mercy. Ines must decide whose survival the truth will cost. Beat: the moral climax approaches — she chooses to speak, but on her own terms.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, climax. The night before demolition, Ines holds a final dinner in the empty Miramar dining room and reads Lucia's letters aloud — to Aurelio, Beatriz, the staff, and the journalist. No one is spared; no one is condemned. Beat: catharsis; grief spoken out loud at last.

chapters.title: A Spoonful of Soup
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, resolution. The hotel falls; her final review publishes — not an exposé but an obituary that tells the whole truth gently. Aurelio serves her a bowl of Lucia's caldo verde. She tastes it. Beat: survival's price paid, and something like grace.
